key_terms.meaning: Main spanwise beam of a wing; its caps (upper and lower flanges) take bending and its web takes shear.
Chordwise member that holds the wing's shape, supports the skin and stringers, and passes load into the spars.
Small longitudinal stiffener riveted to the skin; it carries axial bending stress and stops the skin buckling.
Heavy longitudinal fuselage member, often a main bending member, stronger than a stringer.
Outer sheet that takes air pressure, shear and part of the bending; with the spar webs it closes the wing torsion box.
A heavy transverse member that closes a section, carries concentrated loads, or holds cabin pressure.
Transverse fuselage ring that keeps the cross-section shape and supports stringers and skin.
Transverse beam under the cabin floor that carries floor and passenger loads into the frames.
Extra plate riveted around a cut-out or joint to replace the strength removed by the hole.
Local machined or forged part that joins one member to another and spreads a concentrated load.
Construction in which the skin alone carries all load; strong but needs a thick, heavy skin.
Skin plus frames, stringers and longerons; the thin skin takes shear, torsion and pressure, the stringers take the axial bending stress.
Closed cell formed by front spar, rear spar, top and bottom skin; resists wing twisting.
Two thin stiff faces separated by a light core, giving high bending stiffness at low weight.
Hexagonal-cell core of foil or paper sheet; its cell walls carry shear between the faces.
The largest load expected in service; the structure must carry it with no permanent damage.
Limit load × factor of safety (usually 1.5); the structure must not fail at this load.
Ratio of total lift to weight, n = L/W; n = 1 in level flight, higher in a pull-out or gust.
Plot of load factor n against speed V, bounded by stall, structural and gust limits; its corners size the wing.
Circumferential pressure stress in a thin cylinder, σ = p·r/t, with p pressure, r radius, t wall thickness.
Reduction of the wing root load by the inertia n m g of the wing, fuel and engines outboard of a section.
n = 1 ± ρ V a U / (2 W/S) for a sharp-edged gust of speed U (before the alleviation factor).
P = −(n W a + M₀)/(l<sub>t</sub> − a): the tailplane load that keeps the aircraft in pitch balance; negative is a download.
σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(σ<sub>x</sub>² − σ<sub>x</sub> σ<sub>h</sub> + σ<sub>h</sub>²), the equivalent stress for a biaxial skin stress state.

takeaways: Every aircraft member is a load path: it collects load from a wider area and hands it to a stronger member until the load reaches a support.
Monocoque skins must be thick to avoid buckling, so real aircraft are semi-monocoque, with stringers taking bending and thin skin taking shear.
A wing behaves as a torsion box and a cantilever beam; ribs keep the box shape and transfer skin loads to the spars.
Sandwich panels give very high bending stiffness for low weight because the faces carry bending and the core carries shear.
Material choice is a trade of strength, stiffness, density, fatigue, temperature, corrosion and cost, never a single property.
Fabrication and joints decide real strength; a riveted or bonded joint, not the plate, is usually the weak point.
Limit load is the worst service load, ultimate load is 1.5 times it, and load factor n = L/W converts flight loads to design loads.
The V-n diagram is bounded by the stall parabola, a flat top at n<sub>max</sub> out to V<sub>D</sub>, and n<sub>min</sub>; any gust point outside it, often at V<sub>C</sub>, becomes the sizing case.
Shear and bending moment come from integrating the net spanwise load from the tip; point masses make the shear jump, and the root moment is usually the largest.
A pressurised fuselage is a beam and a pressure vessel at once: hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, and each flight adds a fatigue cycle.
The tailplane load comes from pitch balance at each V-n corner; it and the tail inertia bend the rear fuselage with a moment that grows from the tail to the wing.
bank_note: Most syllabi ask for the loading of the wing, fuselage and tail unit with numbers, and for the use of the V-n diagram in sizing them. Long answers combine a labelled sketch, the load path through each member, and a calculation with limit and ultimate load, load factor, gust load factor, shear force and bending moment, or skin stresses.

bank.q: Define monocoque and semi-monocoque construction. Explain why the semi-monocoque is used for almost all modern aircraft.
outline: Monocoque: the skin carries all load; it must be thick to resist buckling, so it is heavy
Semi-monocoque: thin skin on frames, stringers and longerons
Skin takes shear, torsion and pressure; stringers and longerons take axial bending stress
Frames keep the cross-section and shorten the buckling length of the skin
Result: high strength for the weight, many load paths, easy repair
answer: Monocoque. In a monocoque shell the skin alone carries every load: bending, shear, torsion and cabin pressure. There is no skeleton of stringers and frames. Early wooden racing aircraft and some rocket casings and drop tanks are built this way.

Why a pure monocoque is heavy. A thin unstiffened shell buckles at a low compressive stress, and the compressed side of a bending fuselage is exactly where that happens. The only cure without stiffeners is a thicker skin. Weight grows in proportion to thickness, so the shell becomes heavy long before its material is fully stressed in tension.
Semi-monocoque. The skin is kept thin and a skeleton is added under it: longitudinal stringers (and, on some aircraft, a few heavier longerons) and transverse frames or rings. Each part has a job:

head: Member
Main job
rows: Shear and torsion, cabin pressure (hoop tension), part of the axial bending stress
Axial bending stress; stiffen the skin against buckling
Heavier axial members; collect load at doors, cut-outs and joints
Hold the round shape; split the skin into short panels; spread concentrated loads

answer.text: Pressure in a semi-monocoque skin, with numbers. A fuselage 2.0 m in diameter (r = 1.0 m) with 1.5 mm skin at 60 kPa differential pressure:
answer.pre:
σ<sub>h</sub> = p r / t = 60 000 × 1.0 / 0.0015 = 40 MPa
σ<sub>l</sub> = p r / (2t) = 20 MPa

answer: The thin skin carries this tension easily; tension does not buckle it. It is the compression from bending that needs the stringers and frames, so the skeleton puts material exactly where buckling would start.

Why the semi-monocoque wins. (1) Strength for weight: stringers and frames raise the buckling stress of thin skin, so the skin can work near its material strength. (2) Fail-safety: many members share the load, so one cracked stringer or skin bay does not collapse the structure. (3) Cut-outs: doors and windows are framed by local members without thickening the whole shell. (4) Production and repair: standard sheet, extrusions and rivets; a damaged bay is patched locally.

Closing check. The skin of both types carries the pressure; the difference is buckling under bending compression. Monocoque fixes it with thickness (heavy), semi-monocoque with a skeleton (light). Modern composite fuselages still follow the semi-monocoque idea, with stringers co-cured into the skin.

bank.q: State the function of a spar, rib, stringer, longeron, frame and bulkhead, and give one place on the aircraft where each is found.
outline: Spar: spanwise wing beam, caps take bending, web takes shear
Rib: chordwise, keeps aerofoil shape, passes skin load to spars
Stringer: skin stiffener, takes axial stress with the skin
Longeron: heavy longitudinal fuselage member
Frame: transverse ring holding fuselage section
Bulkhead: closes a section; pressure bulkhead holds cabin pressure
Each tied to a location
answer: The idea. Each member collects load from a thinner, more flexible neighbour and passes it to a stiffer one, until the load reaches a support. So each member is best described by the load it takes in and the load it passes on.

answer.text: The six members.

head: Member
Function
Where found
rows: Main spanwise beam. Caps (top and bottom flanges) carry bending as axial tension and compression; the thin web carries shear. Front and rear spars with the skins close the torsion box.
Wing, tailplane and fin, root to tip
Chordwise member. Holds the aerofoil shape, supports stringers and skin, passes panel loads into the spars, and brings in local loads (engine pylons, flap tracks, gear).
Across the wing box at regular pitch, e.g. 0.45 m
Light longitudinal stiffener riveted to the skin. Carries axial bending stress with the skin and stops it buckling between ribs or frames.
Inside wing skins (spanwise) and fuselage skin (lengthwise)
Heavier longitudinal member. Carries axial bending load, especially where stringers are cut.
Along door and cut-out edges; main members of light-aircraft fuselages
Transverse ring. Keeps the round shape, shortens skin panels, spreads concentrated loads into the skin.
Fuselage, every 0.5 m or so; heavy frames at wing and tail attachments
Solid or webbed partition. Closes a compartment; a pressure bulkhead holds the cabin pressure end load.
Front and rear of the pressure cabin; firewall behind an engine

answer.text: A numerical check on the spar’s job. A spar root carrying M = 288 kN·m and V = 72 kN, caps 0.40 m apart, web 3 mm:
answer.pre:
cap force  F = M / h = 288 000 / 0.40 = 720 kN (top compression, bottom tension)
web shear  τ = V / (h t) = 72 000 / (0.40 × 0.003) = 60 MPa

answer: How they work together in a wing. Air pressure loads the skin; the skin spans between stringers; stringers span between ribs; ribs pass the load to the spars; spars carry it as shear and bending to the root fittings, which hand it into the heavy fuselage frames.

How they work together in a fuselage. Skin and stringers carry bending as axial stress and pressure as hoop tension; frames keep the shell round so the stringers do not buckle; floor beams carry cabin loads to the frames; bulkheads close the pressure vessel at both ends.
Common confusions. Ribs run chordwise and spars spanwise; frames are rings and longerons run lengthwise; a frame is an open ring, a bulkhead is a closed wall.
Closing check. Every member named has one main load and one place: if you can say what it takes in and what it passes on, the answer is complete.

bank.q: Define limit load, ultimate load, factor of safety and load factor. State the usual values used in aircraft design and explain what each means physically.
outline: Limit load: largest load expected in service; no harmful permanent deformation
Ultimate load = 1.5 × limit load; no failure
Factor of safety covers scatter in load, material and analysis
Load factor n = L/W; 1 in level flight, 2.5 typical transport limit
Worked numbers
answer: Load factor n. n = L/W, lift divided by weight; dimensionless. In steady level flight n = 1. In a pull-up the wing must lift more than the weight, and every mass on the aircraft feels n times its weight as an inertia load. A push-over gives n below 1 and can make it negative.

Limit load. The largest load expected in service, from the worst manoeuvre, gust or landing the rules require. At limit load the structure may deflect but must not yield or deform permanently in a harmful way. For transport aircraft the limit manoeuvre load factor is at least 2.5 (and −1.0); light aircraft use about 3.8.
Factor of safety. A multiplier of 1.5 applied to the limit load. It covers small variations in loads, material strength, manufacture and analysis; it is not a cover for gross errors.
Ultimate load. Ultimate load = 1.5 × limit load. The structure must carry it, at least briefly, without failing.

answer.text: Numbers. An aircraft of mass 60 000 kg at n = 2.5 (g = 9.81 m/s²):

answer: What each means physically. n is how heavy the aircraft feels: at 2.5 a 70 kg passenger presses on the seat with 2.5 × 70 × 9.81 = 1717 N. Limit is the worst the aircraft should ever meet; the gap to ultimate is the margin against uncertainty. Stresses at limit load are compared with yield; stresses at ultimate load with ultimate strength.
Closing check. 2207.3 ÷ 1471.5 = 1.5 and 1471.5 ÷ 588.6 = 2.5. Do not apply 1.5 twice, and do not confuse n (a flight condition) with 1.5 (a design multiplier).

bank.q: Describe a typical wing structure with a labelled sketch, and trace the path taken by the lift force from the skin to the wing root.
outline: Two-spar torsion box: front and rear spars, top and bottom skins
Ribs, stringers, leading and trailing edge structure
Pressure on skin to stringers to ribs to spars
Spar caps take bending, webs take shear, closed box takes torsion
Root fittings into fuselage frames and carry-through
Sketch
answer: The layout. A transport wing is a two-spar box. The front spar sits near 15 % of the chord and the rear spar near 60 %; with the top and bottom skins they enclose a closed cell, the torsion box. Ribs cross the box chordwise at a regular pitch. Stringers run spanwise on the inside of both skins. The leading edge (ahead of the front spar) and trailing edge (behind the rear spar) are light structures carrying slats, flaps and ailerons.

svg.aria: Plan view of a wing panel with front and rear spars, six ribs, dashed stringers and a root fitting, and below it the load path chain from air pressure to the fuselage.

answer: Step 1, skin. Air pressure acts normally on the skin. A panel 0.6 m × 0.4 m at 15 kPa carries P = 15 000 × 0.24 = 3600 N. The skin spans between stringers like a small plate.
Step 2, stringers. The skin passes the load to the stringers on either side; four stringers sharing equally carry 900 N each. Stringers span between ribs as small beams.

Step 3, ribs. At each rib the stringers hand their load on. The rib, a deep chordwise web, carries it to the front and rear spar webs. Ribs also keep the aerofoil shape so the skin and stringers do not buckle.

Step 4, spars. The spars collect the load from every rib and carry it inboard. Shear goes in the webs; bending goes in the caps and in the skin-stringer panels as compression on top and tension underneath. With M = 288 kN·m at the root and caps 0.40 m apart, each cap carries F = M/h = 720 kN.

Step 5, torsion. The lift acts ahead of or behind the flexural axis, and the wing has a nose-down pitching moment, so the wing twists. The closed box carries the twist as shear flow round the cell (skins and both webs).

Step 6, root. Root fittings (or a continuous centre box through the fuselage) pass the shear, bending moment and torque into heavy fuselage frames and the carry-through structure, which balances the left and right wings against each other.

Closing check. Load moves from thin, flexible members to thick, stiff ones: 3600 N on one panel becomes 720 kN in each root cap. Mass relief from the wing’s own weight and fuel reduces the root values, which is why the net load, not lift alone, is integrated for the root design.

bank.q: A wing of semi-span 10 m carries a lift that varies linearly from 16 kN/m at the root to 8 kN/m at the tip. Wing structure weighs 2 kN/m along the span, and an engine gives a 30 kN downward load 4 m from the root. Treating the wing as a cantilever, find the shear force and bending moment along the span and sketch both diagrams.
outline: Net load w(x) = 14 − 0.8x kN/m
V(x) = integral of w from x to the tip, minus the engine load inboard of it
M(x) = integral of w times arm, minus engine load times arm
Values at the root, the engine station and the tip
Sketch: shear jump at the engine, moment slope change
answer: Net load. Lift is 16 − 0.8x kN/m (16 at x = 0, 8 at x = 10). Subtracting the 2 kN/m of structure gives the net load w(x) = 14 − 0.8x kN/m, upward, with x from the root.

answer.text: Shear force. Integrate the net load from x to the tip, then subtract the engine load at stations inboard of it:
Bending moment. With u = ξ − x the integral gives a closed form; the engine adds −30(4 − x) inboard of it:
Values along the span.
Root values in full.
Sketch.

svg.aria: Shear force and bending moment along a 10 m semi-span: shear 70 kN at the root, jumping between 20.4 and 50.4 kN at the engine at 4 m, zero at the tip; moment 313.3 kN·m at the root, 136.8 kN·m at 4 m, zero at the tip.

answer: Reading the diagrams. Both are zero at the free tip. The shear grows inboard at the rate w(x), drops by 30 kN at the engine, then grows again to 70 kN at the root. The moment has no jump at the engine, only a change of slope, because a point load changes the shear, which is the slope of M. Here the root has the largest shear (70 kN) but the shear just outboard of the engine (50.4 kN) is higher than at x = 2 m (43.6 kN).

Closing check. Total net load = ∫₀¹⁰ (14 − 0.8x) dx − 30 = 140 − 40 − 30 = 70 kN = V(0). Without the engine the root moment would be 433.3 kN·m; the engine relieves 120 kN·m (28 %). The stated sign convention (upward positive, x from the root) is kept throughout.

svg.aria: V-n diagram: positive stall parabola to corner A at 101 m/s and n 2.5, flat top to D at 175 m/s, vertical line to E, negative limit minus 1 to F at 140 m/s, negative stall curve, and dashed gust lines from n 1 at zero speed, the upward gust at V<sub>C</sub> reaching 2.67.

answer.text: Points for sizing.

head: Point
V (m/s)
n
Use
rows: positive bending at the lowest speed; high angle of attack, centre of pressure forward
largest positive n: sizes root bending
positive bending at highest speed; largest nose-down pitching moment, so torsion
negative bending; top skin in tension, bottom in compression
torsion at V<sub>D</sub> with no lift

answer: Result. The upward gust at VC gives n = 2.67, 6.9 % above the manoeuvre limit, so the gust point sizes the wing for upward bending; the VD corner sizes the torsion box. The downward gusts (−0.67, −0.05) lie inside the −1.0 limit, so F sizes negative bending.

Closing check. At VA the stall line gives (101.0 ÷ 63.9)² = 2.50, as it should; the gust line at VC is above nmax (2.67 > 2.5), so it extends the envelope there. With a gust alleviation factor below 1 the gust point would fall, and the manoeuvre corner might govern instead.

bank.q: A sandwich panel has 0.6 mm aluminium faces (E = 70 GPa) on a 25 mm honeycomb core of density 48 kg/m³. Compare its bending stiffness per metre width with a solid aluminium sheet of the same face mass, and with one of the same total mass. Explain why the sandwich is so much stiffer and what limits it.
outline: D = E t<sub>f</sub> d²/2 with d = core + one face
Solid sheet D = E t³/12
Equal face mass and equal total mass comparisons
Faces carry bending as a couple, core carries shear and spaces the faces
Limits: face wrinkling, core shear, crushing, debonding

answer.text: Sandwich stiffness. The faces act as flanges a distance d apart; their own small bending term is dropped:
Solid sheet of the same face mass (thickness 2 × 0.6 = 1.2 mm):
Solid sheet of the same total mass. Mass per square metre:

answer: Why. Second moment of area grows with distance squared. In a solid sheet most material sits near the neutral axis; in the sandwich all the strong material is at d/2 from it. Each face has I = tf (d/2)² per unit width, and two faces give tf d²/2. The core weighs little but holds the faces apart and carries the transverse shear, like the web of an I-beam.

What limits it. (1) Face wrinkling: the compressed face buckles locally into a soft core, often below yield. (2) Core shear: core shear stress is about V/d, and cores are weak in shear. (3) Core crushing under local loads such as bolts, jacks or a heel, so holes get potted inserts. (4) Debonding of face from core, from poor surface preparation or moisture. (5) Honeycomb is anisotropic: ribbon direction must be specified.

Closing check. Even after paying for the core, the panel is 543 times stiffer than a solid sheet of equal mass, and 1.36 times heavier than its faces alone (4.536 ÷ 3.336). Doubling the core depth would raise D by about (50.6/25.6)² = 3.9 for only 1.2 kg/m² more.

bank.q: A circular fuselage of mean radius 1.9 m and skin thickness 1.8 mm is pressurised to 58 kPa differential and carries a bending moment of 1.2 MN·m. Treating the section as a plain skin tube, compute the skin stresses at the top and bottom, the von Mises stress, and state which stress drives the fatigue life.
outline: Hoop σ<sub>h</sub> = p r/t; longitudinal σ<sub>l</sub> = p r/(2t)
I = π r³ t; σ<sub>b</sub> = M r/I
Superpose at top (tension) and bottom (compression)
Von Mises on both sides
Compression side: buckling; hoop stress cycles each flight: fatigue

answer.text: Pressure stresses.
Bending stress. Thin-tube second moment of area:
Superposition. Assume the moment puts the top in tension (sagging under a tail download reverses this, but the magnitudes are the same):
Von Mises.

answer: The two sides give the same value because σ<sub>l</sub> is exactly σ<sub>h</sub>/2, so the tension and compression values of σ<sub>x</sub> sit equally either side of σ<sub>h</sub>/2. Against 2024-T3 (yield about 345 MPa) the margin is large at this load.

Compression side. The bottom skin carries −28.2 MPa along the fuselage. A thin skin buckles at low stress, so stringers and frames are spaced to keep the panels from buckling; the check is a plate-buckling check, not a von Mises check.

Fatigue driver. Every flight takes the cabin from 0 to 58 kPa and back: one full cycle of 61.2 MPa hoop stress, tens of thousands of times in a service life. Bending stresses vary with gusts and manoeuvres, but the pressure cycle is the large, regular one. Hoop stress opens cracks that run along the fuselage, so lap joints along the fuselage and the corners of windows and doors are the classic fatigue sites. Tear straps and crack-stopper frames limit crack length, and inspections are planned on crack-growth rates (damage tolerance).
Closing check. σh = 2σl (61.22 = 2 × 30.61). The real fuselage has stringers, so I is larger and σb smaller than the plain-tube value; the pressure stresses stay with the skin alone.

bank.q: Explain how a riveted lap joint in a fuselage skin carries load, list the failure modes an engineer checks, and find the strength of a joint of two 1.6 mm sheets, 100 mm wide, joined by two rows of four 4 mm rivets (allowables: rivet shear 200 MPa, bearing 480 MPa, net tension 290 MPa).
outline: Load passes from sheet to rivet by bearing, across the rivet by shear, into the second sheet
Checks: rivet shear, bearing, net-section tension, edge tear-out
Row load sharing: end rows take more; first row is the net-section critical line
Eccentricity of a single lap; fatigue at holes
Numerical joint strength and efficiency
answer: How the load is carried. Tension in the upper sheet presses against the rivet shanks (bearing). Each rivet is cut across the joint plane (single shear in a lap joint). The lower sheet takes the load back by bearing on the other side of the rivets. Friction from the rivet clamp carries a little, but design ignores it.

Failure modes checked. (1) Rivet shear across the faying plane. (2) Bearing: the hole elongates in the thinner sheet. (3) Net-section tension through the line of holes. (4) Edge tear-out, prevented by keeping an edge distance of about 2d. (5) Fatigue cracking from hole edges under repeated pressurisation.

answer.text: Numbers. 8 rivets, d = 4 mm (A = 12.57 mm²), t = 1.6 mm, w = 100 mm:

head: Mode
Working
Load (N)
rows: Net section at the first row

answer: Strength = 20.1 kN, in rivet shear. Efficiency = 20 106 ÷ 46 400 = 43 %. The net section is checked at the first row, because that row carries the whole sheet load past its holes; the second row sees only what the first row has not already transferred.

Load sharing and eccentricity. Rows do not share equally: the outer rows take more because the sheets stretch between rows. In a single lap the two sheets are offset by one thickness, so the joint bends and the rivet heads pry; that is why fuselage longitudinal laps use three rows, or butt joints with a doubler.

Fatigue. The hole is a stress raiser and the bending of the lap adds stress at the faying surface. Countersunk holes in thin outer skin are especially sensitive, and multi-site damage along a lap row is a known airliner hazard. Sealant and bonding (rivet-bonding) reduce the load per rivet; cold-worked holes and interference fits slow crack growth.
Closing check. Ultimate design load must stay below 20.1 kN; a larger rivet or a third row would move the critical mode toward bearing and raise the efficiency.

bank.q: Compare aluminium alloy, titanium alloy and carbon fibre composite for a wing upper skin. Justify a choice and state the trade-offs involved.
outline: Upper skin is compression- and buckling-critical, with fatigue, damage and repair concerns
Specific strength and stiffness; buckling index E<sup>1/3</sup>/ρ
Aluminium: cheap, proven, repairable, ~25 MN·m/kg
Titanium: strong, hot, costly, heavy for buckling
CFRP: high stiffness for weight, impact damage, temperature, lightning, galvanic
Reasoned choice
answer: What the upper skin needs. In upward bending the upper skin is in compression, so it is designed by panel buckling and compressive strength, not tensile strength. It also needs damage tolerance (tool drops, hail), fuel-tank sealing, lightning protection and repairability.

answer.text: Data (typical values; CFRP as a quasi-isotropic skin laminate, E about 50 GPa, strength about 600 MPa):

answer: Why E1/3/ρ. A skin panel of given width and length carrying a given compressive load buckles at a stress proportional to E t². For a fixed load, the lightest panel minimises ρ t, which leads to a mass proportional to ρ/E1/3. So a higher E1/3/ρ (units: GPa1/3 per tonne/m³) means a lighter buckling-critical skin.

Aluminium. E1/3/ρ = 1.47. Cheap, easy to form, machine and rivet, inspectable, repairable at any airfield. 7075 or 7150-type alloys suit the compression skin. Drawbacks: corrosion, fatigue at holes, and no gain on stiffness over other metals.

Titanium. High strength, good fatigue and corrosion resistance, keeps strength hot. But E1/3/ρ = 1.10, worst of the three, because its density is 1.6 times aluminium’s while its modulus is only 1.6 times higher, and the cube root weakens the modulus benefit. It is also costly and slow to machine. Titanium suits hot zones and highly loaded fittings, not a large skin.

CFRP. E1/3/ρ = 2.30, about 55 % better than aluminium, so the skin can be much lighter; plies can be laid to suit the loads, and it does not corrode or fatigue like metal. But impact damage can hide inside, compression after impact sets the allowable (lowering the usable strength), lightning needs a metal mesh, joints to aluminium need galvanic isolation, repairs need bonding and controlled cure, and the material and certification are costly.

Choice. For a high-production airliner today, CFRP gives the lightest upper skin and is used on the newest wide-bodies; for a smaller aircraft, or where cost, repair and proven practice matter most, a 7000-series aluminium skin is the sensible choice. Titanium is not chosen for the skin.
Closing check. The ranking reverses depending on the property: on σ/ρ titanium beats aluminium, on E1/3/ρ it loses. A sound answer names the governing failure mode first and then picks the material.

bank.q: A semi-monocoque fuselage of radius 1.9 m at 55 kPa differential pressure is cut for a cargo door 1.8 m long and 2.0 m high. Analyse the effect on the structure, and evaluate the role of doublers, frames, sills and crack stoppers in restoring strength.
outline: Cut-out removes skin and stringers; loads must go round
Hoop load N = p r per metre of length; longitudinal p r/2 per metre of height
Stress concentration at corners; radii
Edge frames, sill and header beams, doublers
Door plug loads; crack stoppers; fatigue
answer: What the cut removes. Skin, several stringers and parts of frames. The shell had carried hoop tension, longitudinal tension, bending stress and shear through that area. All of it must now go round the opening, and the door itself, unless it is a plug type, carries little.

answer.text: Size of the diverted loads. Hoop tension per metre of fuselage length is Nh = p r; longitudinal tension per metre of height is Nl = p r / 2:

answer: Where the loads go. The 188 kN of hoop tension goes into the two heavy edge frames at the forward and aft sides of the door. The 104.5 kN of longitudinal tension, plus the fuselage bending load of the cut stringers, goes into the sill (below) and header (above) beams, which act as heavy longerons. The shear that the cut skin carried passes round the frame of members as a stiff picture frame.

Corners. Where these members meet, the stress concentrates. A sharp corner can raise the local stress several times; generous radii and corner doublers keep it low. Corners are the classic fatigue sites.
Doublers. Extra skin bonded or riveted round the opening restores area and spreads the load from the edge members into the surrounding skin over a longer length, so the rivet rows are not overloaded.

Crack stoppers. Tear straps and frames act as barriers: a crack growing from a corner meets extra material and slows or turns. This makes the design fail-safe, and inspection intervals are set from crack-growth rates.

The door. A plug door, larger than its opening, is pressed into the frame by pressure and carries its pressure load in bearing on stops. A cargo door usually opens outward, so its latches carry the full pressure load: 55 000 × 1.8 × 2.0 = 198 kN. Latch failure is catastrophic, so latches have indicators and redundancy.

Evaluation. A well-framed opening returns the section close to its uncut strength, but always at a weight cost (heavy frames, sills, doublers) and with new fatigue sites. The design is acceptable only when the static check of the edge members and a fatigue and damage-tolerance analysis of the corners both pass.
Closing check. Nl = Nh/2 as for a closed cylinder; the edge frames carry about 94 kN each (188 ÷ 2).

bank.q: An aircraft of weight 600 kN has a wing weighing 60 kN and a semi-span of 15 m. Its V-n diagram gives a manoeuvre limit of 2.5 and a gust point of 2.84 at V<sub>C</sub>. Using a uniform spanwise net load, size the bending material at the wing root for an effective box depth of 0.6 m and an allowable stress of 450 MPa at ultimate load. Evaluate how raising the limit load factor to 3.0, or raising the aspect ratio at the same wing area, alters the design.
outline: Design n is the highest corner: gust 2.84
Net lift per half-wing n(W − W<sub>wing</sub>)/2, uniform over the semi-span
Root M = w L²/2; ultimate = 1.5 × limit
Bending material area A = M/(h σ) on each side of the box
Effect of n = 3.0
Effect of aspect ratio: span up, chord and depth down
answer: Step 1, design load factor. The wing must cover every point of the envelope. The upward gust at VC (2.84) is above the manoeuvre limit (2.5), so n = 2.84 is used for upward bending.

answer.text: Step 2, net load on one half-wing. Fuselage, payload and fuel outside the wing are carried by the lift; the wing’s own weight relieves itself (mass relief):
answer.pre:
net lift per half-wing = n (W − W<sub>wing</sub>) / 2 = 2.84 × (600 − 60) / 2 = 766.8 kN
uniform net load      w = 766.8 / 15 = 51.12 kN/m

answer.text: Step 3, root bending moment.
answer.pre:
limit    M = w L² / 2 = 51.12 × 15² / 2 = 5751 kN·m
ultimate M = 1.5 × 5751              = 8626.5 kN·m

answer: A real lift distribution is closer to elliptic, whose centre of lift on each half-wing sits at 4L/(3π) = 0.424L instead of 0.5L, so the uniform assumption overestimates the root moment by about 18 %: it is a conservative first estimate.

answer.text: Step 4, bending material. Top and bottom of the box act as a couple h = 0.6 m apart:
answer.pre:
force in each side   F = M / h = 8 626 500 / 0.6 = 14 377.5 kN
area needed          A = F / σ = 14 377 500 / (450 × 10⁶) = 0.03195 m² = 31 950 mm²

answer: This area is shared by the front and rear spar caps and the skin-stringer panels between them on each side. Over a box width of, say, 2.0 m it is an equivalent thickness of 31 950 ÷ 2000 = 16 mm, typical of a mid-size airliner’s root. The compression side must also pass panel buckling, and the tension side must pass fatigue at limit load.

answer.text: Step 5, raising n to 3.0.

answer: Root moment and material area grow in direct proportion to n: 3.0 ÷ 2.84 = 1.056, so 5.6 % more bending material. Wing weight then grows, which slightly increases the relief and the total weight: a small spiral.

Step 6, raising aspect ratio at the same area. AR = b²/S. Raising the span by 20 % (L = 18 m) at the same area raises AR by 1.2² = 1.44 and cuts the mean chord by 1.2. For the same total lift, uniform loading gives M = (lift per half-wing) × L/2, so M rises by 20 %. The box depth scales with chord, so h falls by 1.2. Area needed ∝ M/h rises by 1.2 × 1.2 = 1.44, a 44 % heavier bending structure.

Evaluation. Higher aspect ratio cuts induced drag, which is why airliner wings are long and slender, but it is paid for in root bending material roughly in proportion to the aspect ratio; composites, deeper aerofoil sections at the root, and load alleviation are used to recover the weight. A higher limit load factor costs weight almost linearly and is accepted only where the role (aerobatic, military) needs it.

bank.q: Describe how loads from the tail unit are transferred into the rear fuselage, and analyse why the rear fuselage is often critical for bending and fatigue. Use an aircraft of weight 500 kN at n = 2.5 with the wing lift 0.5 m behind the CG, a tail arm of 15 m, a tail-unit mass of 800 kg and a fin side load of 30 kN at 2.5 m above the fuselage axis (r = 1.2 m, skin 1.6 mm). Compare wing pitching moments of 150 kN·m (at V<sub>A</sub>) and 300 kN·m (at V<sub>D</sub>).
outline: Tailplane balancing load from pitch equilibrium; fin side load from rudder or sideslip
Loads enter through fittings and heavy frames
Rear-fuselage shear and moment grow forward from the tail
Fin load gives torsion T = F h, shear flow q = T/2A
Why critical: long arm, smaller section, cut-outs, load reversal and fatigue
answer: How tail loads enter. The tailplane spars end at fittings on heavy frames in the rear fuselage (or, on a T-tail, on the fin spars, which pass the load down into the fuselage). The fin spars attach to two or three heavy frames. These frames spread the concentrated fitting loads into the skin as shear flow.

answer.text: Tailplane balancing load. P = −(n W a + M₀)/(lt − a), with n W a = 2.5 × 500 × 0.5 = 625 kN·m and lt − a = 14.5 m:

answer: The higher speed corner gives the larger tail download, because the wing’s nose-down pitching moment grows with dynamic pressure. This is how the V-n corners size the tail.

answer.text: Rear-fuselage bending. Tail inertia n m g = 2.5 × 800 × 9.81 = 19.62 kN adds to the download. At a frame 10 m forward of the tail:

answer: The moment is zero at the tail and grows linearly forward to the wing attachment. On a plain 1.2 m tube with 3.0 mm equivalent thickness (I = 0.01629 m⁴), the V<sub>D</sub> case gives σ = 834 100 × 1.2 ÷ 0.01629 = 61.4 MPa.

answer.text: Fin load. The side load bends the fuselage sideways and twists it:
answer.pre:
torque     T = F h = 30 × 2.5 = 75 kN·m
enclosed   A = π r² = π × 1.2² = 4.524 m²
shear flow q = T / (2A) = 75 000 / 9.048 = 8289 N/m
skin shear τ = q / t = 8289 / 0.0016 = 5.18 MPa

answer: Why the rear fuselage is critical. (1) The tail loads act on the longest lever arm on the aircraft, so modest forces make large moments. (2) The rear fuselage tapers, so its section (and I) is smaller just where the moment is applied. (3) It has cut-outs: rear doors, service panels, and on some aircraft an APU bay or a tail cone opening. (4) Loads reverse: balancing loads, gusts and manoeuvres swing the tail load up and down and the fin load left and right, so each skin panel sees alternating tension and compression. (5) Pressure cycles add hoop stress every flight, and the rear pressure bulkhead sits here. Fatigue cracks therefore start at fitting holes and frame-to-skin joints; damage-tolerance inspections concentrate on the rear pressure bulkhead and tail attachment frames.
Closing check. Moments about the CG for the VD case: −1313.8 × 0.5 − 300 + 63.79 × 15 = −656.9 − 300 + 956.9 = 0.

glossary.def: The continuous route by which a force travels from where it is applied to the support that reacts it.
A transverse wall-like member that closes a section, carries concentrated load, or holds cabin pressure.
A transverse ring in the fuselage that maintains the cross-section shape and supports stringers and skin.
A small longitudinal stiffener on the inside of the skin that takes axial stress and delays skin buckling.
A heavy longitudinal fuselage member that acts as a main bending member.
The upper or lower flange of a spar, farthest from the neutral axis, carrying the largest bending stress.
A chordwise wing member that gives the aerofoil shape and transfers skin and stringer loads to the spars.
An extra plate added around a cut-out or joint to restore the strength taken away.
A local machined or forged component that connects two members and spreads a concentrated load.
Construction where the skin alone carries all loads, with no internal skeleton.
Construction with thin skin supported by frames, stringers and longerons so that each carries part of the load.
A closed cell of spars and skin that resists twisting of a wing or tail surface.
Two thin stiff faces bonded to a thick light core to obtain high bending stiffness at low weight.
A core of hexagonal cells, made from foil or paper, whose walls carry shear between the faces.
The maximum load expected in service, which the structure must carry without permanent damage.
Limit load multiplied by the factor of safety, usually 1.5; the structure must not fail at this value.
The ratio n = L/W of lift to weight, which measures how many times the aircraft feels heavier than its weight.
A graph of load factor against equivalent airspeed showing the flight envelope and the critical design cases.
The extra lift created when the aircraft meets an upward or downward air current.
The circumferential tensile stress in a pressurised cylinder, equal to p·r/t.
The line in a beam section where bending stress is zero and about which the bending stresses balance.
Sudden sideways deflection of a thin member under compression at a load below its crushing strength.
Failure by repeated load cycles that start and grow a crack at a stress concentration.
Design in which a crack or failed member is stopped by other members until it is found in inspection.
